title: Bias variance tradeoff
story:
Two quite different failures both arrive as error on unseen data, and a single error number adds them together without saying which you have.

The first is being systematically wrong. Your model's form cannot represent the relationship — a line through a curve — so it misses in the same direction every time, and it would go on missing in that direction however much data you collected. That is bias, and it is a property of what you assumed rather than of the sample.

The second is being unstable. Your model's form could represent the relationship, but the particular fit you obtained is chasing the sample you happened to draw. Draw a different sample and you get a noticeably different model with different predictions. That is variance, and it is a property of the sample rather than of the assumption.

Geman, Bienenstock and Doursat set this out in 1992, examining the dual sources of estimation error and showing it decomposes into these two components: large numbers of parameter estimates raise the variance, whereas incorrect statistical models increase the bias. Their framing is the useful one and it is in the title — a dilemma rather than a choice. The tension is stated directly: model-free approaches assume no particular geometric structure, use many parameters and exhibit high estimation variance, while controlling that variance requires model-based architectures that may increase modelling bias.

Read that as the structural statement it is. Every assumption you impose to stabilise an estimate is an assumption that can be wrong. Restricting to lines makes your fit stable across samples and wrong if the truth is curved. Permitting any shape makes you right in principle and unstable in practice. You are not choosing a point on a dial marked accuracy; you are choosing how much of your error comes from what you assumed against how much comes from which rows you happened to get.

The practical asymmetry worth carrying is how each responds to more data. Variance shrinks — a larger sample pins the estimate down, and the model you fit stops moving when the sample changes. Bias does not shrink at all. A line fitted to a curve on a million rows is a very precisely estimated line, and it is exactly as wrong about the curve as before. This is the same distinction that appeared under sampling: collecting more addresses one failure and leaves the other untouched, which is why the first question about a disappointing model is which of the two it has, not how much more data you can get.

problem.name: The bias-variance decomposition
problem.shape: A model performs poorly on unseen data, and the error has two sources that call for opposite responses.
tell: the model misses in the same direction across the whole range
refitting on a different sample gives noticeably different predictions
more data has been collected and nothing improved
regularisation is being tuned without a view on which error dominates
problem.move: Decide which component dominates before acting. Refit on resamples and look at how much the predictions move — that movement is variance. Look at the residuals for structure the model cannot express — that pattern is bias. Add data or reduce capacity for the first; change the model's form or add features for the second.
problem.invariant: Estimation error decomposes into a bias component, from the model's form, and a variance component, from the sample. More data reduces variance and leaves bias exactly where it was.
problem.breaks: The two cannot be reduced independently by the same means. Assuming less raises variance and assuming more raises bias, so past the point where both are being addressed, every reduction in one is paid for in the other — which is why it is described as a dilemma rather than a setting to optimise.

cost.time: refitting on resamples to measure how much the model moves, which is the only direct way to see the variance component
cost.beats: tuning against a single held-out number, which reports the sum of the two and gives no indication of which one you are changing

worked.problem: Why does collecting more data fix one of these and not the other?
worked.reasoning:
Because one component is a property of the sample and the other is a property of what you assumed, and more data is more sample.

Variance is the extent to which your fitted model depends on which rows you happened to draw. It exists because the sample is finite: with few observations, the fit chases their particular noise, and a different draw produces a noticeably different model. Enlarging the sample pins the estimate down — the noise averages out, successive samples look more alike, and the fitted models converge. So variance shrinks with data, and in the limit it goes to zero.

Bias is the extent to which the best possible member of your model class differs from the truth. Fit a line to a curved relationship and the line will miss in the same direction in the same places, and enlarging the sample does not change that. It makes you more certain about which line is best — a very precisely estimated line — and the best line is still not a curve. Nothing about having more rows enlarges the set of shapes your model can express, and bias is entirely about that set.

This is the same distinction that appears in sampling, where noise shrinks with more observations and bias does not, and it is worth noticing that it recurs for the same underlying reason: collecting more of something addresses the randomness of what you collected and never addresses whether you were measuring the right thing.

The practical consequence is a diagnostic order. If a model is disappointing, the first question is which component dominates, because it determines whether more data is worth acquiring at all. Refit on several resamples and see how much the predictions move: large movement means variance, and more data will help. Look at the residuals for systematic structure — curvature, a pattern in one region, consistent under-prediction of a subgroup: that is bias, and more of the same data will not touch it. What will is changing the model's form, adding features that express the missing structure, or reducing regularisation if you have constrained it too far.

And the reason this is framed as a dilemma rather than a dial: the means of reducing each one work against the other. Restricting the model to stabilise it imposes an assumption that may be wrong; loosening it to remove that assumption makes it chase the sample. Once you are past the easy gains, every reduction in one is paid for in the other.

problem.practice: Fit the same model on ten resamples of your data and plot all ten sets of predictions on one axis — the width of that band is the variance. Then plot the residuals of a single fit against each feature and look for structure. Decide which component dominates before you next change anything.

beats.broke: Two different things both appear as error on unseen data — being systematically wrong, and being unstable — and a single error number adds them together without saying which you have.
beats.fix: Decompose the estimation error into a bias component, from the model's form being wrong, and a variance component, from the estimate moving with the sample, and treat them as separate quantities with separate remedies.
beats.cost: They cannot both be reduced by the same means: assuming less raises variance and assuming more raises bias, so past a point every reduction in one is paid for in the other.

interview.q: Why does collecting more data fix one of these and not the other?
interview.trap: Treating more data as a general remedy for poor performance. It shrinks the component caused by the finiteness of the sample and leaves untouched the component caused by the model's form — a line fitted to a curve on a million rows is a precisely estimated line and just as wrong.
interview.answer:
Because one component is a property of the sample and the other is a property of what you assumed, and more data is more sample.
